w:r.w:t: A Support System for Car Recognition, Valuation and Recommendation in Vietnam
FSB Institute of Management and Technology, FPT University,

This report describes a working prototype that supports three questions that buyers of second-hand cars in Vietnam ask repeatedly: which listings match what I am looking for, what vehicle does this photograph show, and is the asking price reasonable for this year of production and this distance on the odometer. The three features are decoupled pipelines that share one listing table. Text search applies regular expressions that turn a Vietnamese request into explicit attributes such as brand, price band, production year, seat count and body style, and then ranks the surviving listings by fusing a multilingual MiniLM sentence embedding with a TF-IDF representation. Image recognition uses MobileNetV2 pre-trained on ImageNet with a compact classification head and a confidence gate that refuses to answer when the network is not sure. Price analysis fits single-variable ordinary least squares models to production year and odometer reading under a grouped hold-out split. All three components were evaluated on 15,442 Vietnamese listings and on a seven-class collection of 4,165 vehicle photographs; the classifier reaches 97.05% accuracy and 96.54% macro-F1 on 813 unseen images, while the two regressions explain less than 5% of the price variance and are therefore reported as descriptive market references rather than as valuation models.

The Vietnamese second-hand car market has moved almost entirely online, but the information a buyer works with is still mostly unstructured: a title, a free-text description, a photograph, a price, and a handful of fields that the seller filled in inconsistently or left blank. Keyword search over such a collection is fragile for two reasons. First, buyers describe a car the way they talk about it, so that one request is written as “Toyota Innova 2020 7 chỗ”, “innova 2020 7 seat” or “xe 7 chỗ đời 2020”, and a literal substring match finds only part of the intended set. Second, the most discriminative tokens in that vocabulary are short alphanumeric codes: a buyer who writes “C200” wants the C200, and a model that has learned that “Mercedes” is close to “Mercedes” will happily return the adjacent C300 AMG trim.

Two further pieces of information are missing from the listing itself. A photograph identifies the vehicle category more reliably than the seller’s own text, and the price carries information that the seller does not spell out. Year of production and distance travelled are the two variables Vietnamese buyers trust most, yet neither is easy to interpret without a sense of how prices are distributed for comparable cars. This report builds one prototype that addresses the three gaps at once, and it is deliberately modular: a hybrid text retrieval engine, a transfer-learned image classifier and two econometric baselines are independent tracks that read the same listing table and are presented in one web interface. The design goal is transparency: every recommendation is accompanied by the parsed criteria, the per-criterion match state of the selected listing and the price trend that produced the chart, so that a user can see where a suggestion comes from and reject it when it does not fit. The report is organised around three research questions:

RQ1. How far does a hybrid retrieval engine that combines rule-based attribute filters, dense multilingual sentence embeddings and sparse TF-IDF matching recover the listings a Vietnamese buyer intends, and where does it fail?

RQ2. How accurately does MobileNetV2 pre-trained on ImageNet separate seven vehicle categories on a held-out test split of 813 photographs, and what does a confidence threshold of 0.60 contribute to the reliability of the answer?

RQ3. How much of the price variation in the listing table can a single-variable ordinary least squares model explain on a grouped hold-out split, and what does that imply about using it to value an individual car?

Text retrieval on short, heterogeneous documents is classically addressed with sparse lexical models. In the tf-idf weighting of Salton and Buckley [13], the weight of a term combines how often it occurs in a document with how widely it is distributed across the collection. The approach remains attractive here because it is transparent, cheap, and matches the alphanumeric vocabulary of car trims exactly: the token “c200” is the same token in the query and in the listing, and no amount of semantic smoothing should blur it. Lexical matching alone, however, fails on the part of the query that carries intent rather than identity. Asking for an SUV with seven seats and a budget of one billion VND expresses constraints, not vocabulary, and a bag of words cannot tell whether the author wanted “SUV” to be satisfied by the body-style field or merely mentioned in the prose. Dense retrieval addresses this directly: Sentence-BERT [12] adapts the pre-trained bidirectional encoder of Devlin et al. [4] into a bi-encoder in which query and document are embedded independently and compared by cosine similarity, and multilingual capability comes from distilling an English teacher into a student trained on translated sentence pairs [11]. The two families are complementary rather than redundant: the embedding captures paraphrase and intent, while the sparse vector captures the exact codes and proper nouns that distinguish one trim from another.

On the visual side, convolutional neural networks learn hierarchical features directly from pixels; the architecture of LeCun et al. [9] is the classical reference. Training such a network from scratch requires far more data than the present task provides, so transfer learning is the practical choice: a backbone pre-trained on ImageNet [3] is reused and only a small classification head is trained on the target domain. MobileNetV2 [14] suits this setting, because its inverted residual blocks keep the representation expressive at low cost, which makes it a good candidate for CPU-only inference. Two training details matter for the results reported later. The first is class re-weighting: the image collection is imbalanced, and the effective-number weighting of Cui et al. [2] gives each class a weight proportional to the inverse of the expected overlap between its samples, milder than plain inverse frequency and better suited to a short fine-tuning schedule. The second is the use of mild augmentation only, because aggressive rotation or cropping removes exactly the grille, badge and headlamp shapes that distinguish the seven brands.

The econometric component is deliberately modest. Ordinary least squares estimates the coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals, and it is the natural first baseline for the relationship between a listing price and a single numeric attribute such as production year or odometer reading. Its value here is not prediction accuracy but orientation: it quantifies how much of the observed price variation is associated with each attribute, and so establishes the limit of what an individual attribute can tell a buyer about a price. The estimates are obtained through the estimator interface of scikit-learn [10], and every reported metric is computed on data withheld from the fit. The split is grouped rather than row-wise: listings that share a name and a price are the same car reposted on several platforms, and a row-wise split would place such near-duplicates on both sides of the boundary and inflate the apparent generalisation of the model.

The primary corpus is a public collection of used-car listings scraped from Vietnamese marketplaces [8]: 15,442 records described by 17 columns, among them the model name, the asking price as free text, the production year, the distance travelled, the body style, the fuel type, the transmission, the number of seats and doors, the colours, the origin, the condition and the location. The free-text price field is the reason the collection needs cleaning before any statistic can be computed: prices appear as “1 Tỷ 118 Triệu”, as “646 Triệu”, or occasionally as a bare number, and the parser converts these forms into a single numeric column in millions of VND. Every listing yields a positive price, so no record is discarded at this stage. The remaining cleaning is conservative. Missing values are never imputed; they are treated as unknown, and a listing whose year is unknown is simply excluded from the year-based analysis. The unknown rates are uneven: distance travelled is unknown for 22.95% of listings, by far the most serious gap, whereas the transmission is recovered from the description text for all but 0.01% of records, and body style, fuel type, production year and seat count are each unknown for 3.57%.

The production year is present for 14,891 listings whose distribution, shown in Fig. 1, is concentrated in the second half of the 2010s, with a median of 2020 and a range from 1989 to 2024. Prices are spread over three orders of magnitude: the median listing is priced at 659 million VND, the mean is pulled up to 1,232 million VND by a few expensive vehicles, and the most expensive record is quoted at 63,568 million VND. Such extremes are retained because they are genuine market observations rather than parsing artefacts, but they mean that any regression on price must be read as descriptive rather than predictive. A further characteristic constrains the interpretation: 3,533 listings share both a model name and a price with an earlier listing, almost certainly the same vehicle reposted on several platforms. The retrieval pipeline removes them from the displayed results and the regression analysis groups them together, so that a repost cannot appear in both the training and the test partition.

The visual component uses a separate public collection of vehicle photographs [7] organised into seven category folders: Audi, Hyundai Creta, Mahindra Scorpio, Rolls Royce, Maruti Suzuki Swift, Tata Safari and Toyota Innova. The publisher splits it into 3,352 training and 813 test photographs, so the test split can be used exactly as published. The class distribution is markedly imbalanced: Audi accounts for 1,013 of the 4,165 images, or 24.3% of the collection, and Toyota Innova for a further 23.2%, so the two largest classes alone represent 47.5% of the data, whereas the smallest class, Hyundai Creta, contributes only 338 images, a factor of three fewer than the largest. A model evaluated on accuracy alone could therefore obtain a respectable score by favouring the majority classes, which is why the balanced accuracy and the macro-averaged F1 score are reported alongside the overall accuracy.

The prototype is a single Streamlit application [15] organised as three decoupled processing tracks that share one in-memory listing table. The separation is not merely cosmetic: each track can fail without taking the others down. If the sentence embedding model cannot be loaded, the retrieval engine falls back to TF-IDF matching and reports the degradation in the interface, while the classifier and the regression charts continue to work. Fig. 2 gives the overall arrangement. Two engineering decisions keep the application responsive on commodity hardware. First, the sentence embeddings of all 15,442 listings and the TF-IDF matrix are computed once and cached on disk; the cache key is a SHA-256 digest of the model name together with a fingerprint of the dataset file, so a change to the data or to the model invalidates the cache automatically while an unchanged file reuses it. Second, the embedding model is loaded lazily, only when a query actually needs semantic scoring. The model itself is the twelve-layer multilingual MiniLM bi-encoder released on the Hugging Face Hub [5], and both the embedding and the inference step run comfortably on a multi-core CPU, so no GPU is required anywhere.

A natural language request in Vietnamese is first converted into a set of explicit criteria. Each criterion records the column it constrains, the comparison operator, the value and a human-readable label shown back to the user, which keeps the extraction step explainable. The parser works with regular expressions on an accent-stripped, lower-cased copy of the query and recognises up to fourteen attributes: location, distance, price, production year, interior colour, exterior colour, fuel type, transmission, origin, condition, seat count, door count, body style and brand. The order in which the query is examined is not arbitrary, because several patterns are ambiguous in isolation. Locations come before fuel type and colour, because a place name such as “Đồng Nai” would otherwise be matched by a colour or fuel pattern. Distance comes before price and year, because the digits “2000” in “2000 km” denote a distance and not a model year. Interior colour comes before exterior colour, because “nội thất màu đen” contains the word for colour but refers to the interior. Once a pattern matches, the span it covered is blanked rather than deleted, so the remaining tokens are not concatenated into spurious matches. Brand detection is the one criterion that does not rely on a fixed list of triggers: an exact, word-boundary match against 28 brand names is tried first, and if that fails the remaining tokens are compared with a character-level similarity measure, a fuzzy match being accepted only when the best score reaches 0.76 and exceeds the second best by at least 0.04.

The extracted criteria are applied as a hard filter. Every criterion must hold simultaneously, and a listing whose value for a constrained attribute is unknown does not satisfy that criterion. The strict filter therefore narrows the 15,442 listings to a candidate set whose size depends entirely on the query: the three benchmark requests of Section 5 leave 3,450, 44 and 287 candidates respectively. a min-max normalised score, exposed as an interface control because the balance it encodes is a design decision rather than a law. A strict filter is in turn brittle in a heterogeneous corpus, so when no listing satisfies all criteria the system falls back through five fixed stages, releasing the price band, then the production year, then the colour, distance, location, fuel, transmission, origin, condition and door-count criteria together, and finally the seat count and the body style. The brand criterion is never released, because a search for a Toyota that returns a Hyundai is not a relaxed result but a wrong answer. Each stage is attempted in turn and the first that yields a candidate is used, so a query that is already satisfiable is never relaxed at all. Relaxation is never silent: the interface names the criteria that were released, and each displayed listing shows the match state of every original criterion.

The classifier is MobileNetV2 with the ImageNet weights and the fully connected top removed, assembled with the Keras API of TensorFlow [1], followed by a classification head consisting of global average pooling, dropout at rate 0.30, a dense layer of 128 units with ReLU activation, a second dropout at rate 0.20 and a softmax output over the seven classes, for 2,422,855 parameters in total. Training proceeds in two stages: five epochs with the backbone frozen at a learning rate of 10⁻³, then fine-tuning of the whole network at 10⁻⁴, with early stopping on validation accuracy. At inference a photograph is converted to RGB, resized to 224 × 224 pixels and scaled to the unit interval exactly as in training, and the softmax output is inspected. A prediction is accepted only when the probability of the leading class reaches a threshold of 0.60; below that value the system reports the result as uncertain instead of naming a class, because a refusal is preferable to a confident wrong answer.

The third track fits ordinary least squares models to the price against production year and against odometer reading and renders the fit together with binned medians and an inter-quartile band, so that the user sees the spread of the market rather than a single line; when a search has already fixed the brand, the analysis is restricted to that brand. The price distribution across body styles complements the regression output: the medians differ by more than an order of magnitude between the cheapest and the most expensive body style, which suggests that body style orients a buyer better than either of the two numeric variables examined here.

The retrieval engine was evaluated on three representative requests, each chosen to exercise a different failure mode of keyword search: a broad category with a budget constraint, a brand and model with an explicit configuration, and a brand with an alphanumeric trim designation. For each request the three retrieval modes were run over the identical candidate set and the top-ranked listing was recorded. Table 1 gives the outcome. The attribute filter behaves as intended: for the Innova query the three extracted criteria reduce the corpus to 44 listings, and all three retrieval modes agree on the same top result, the 2020 Innova V 2.0 with an automatic transmission at 699 million VND.
Top-ranked listing for three benchmark queries under the hybrid, semantic and TF-IDF retrieval modes.

The broad SUV query separates the modes more clearly. The hybrid ranking returns a 2024 Toyota Avanza Premio at 565 million VND, well inside the budget, and the semantic mode returns the same model from 2022 at 520 million VND. The lexical mode behaves differently: it returns a Lynk & Co 01 from 2024 at 999 million VND, the most expensive car in the candidate set, because the query shares the token “SUV” with that listing while the other two vehicles are described with different wording. The hybrid score avoids this failure by giving the semantic component the larger weight, but the example also shows that the lexical score is not a reliable ranking signal on its own. The trim query is the most instructive of the three. The parser extracts the Mercedes-Benz brand and the 2021 model year and leaves 287 candidates, but the requested trim “C200” is not among the parsed criteria, because trim designations are alphanumeric codes that the regular expressions cannot distinguish from one another. Both the hybrid and the semantic mode rank the C300 AMG first, at 1,350 million VND, while only the lexical mode returns the C200 Exclusive at 1,220 million VND. This is the characteristic weakness of a bi-encoder: query and document are embedded independently, so the difference between two adjacent trim codes is smaller than the differences between them and unrelated vehicles. Three observations follow. First, rule-based extraction is reliable when the requested attributes are categorical, numeric or explicitly named. Second, the two representations fail in different ways, which is precisely the argument for fusing them rather than choosing one. Third, the trim confusion is not fixable by re-weighting the fusion: it requires a mechanism that compares query and document jointly, such as a cross-encoder reranking stage or an explicit trim token extracted from the title.

The classifier was evaluated once, on the published test split of 813 photographs that was never used for training or for the validation split. It reaches 97.05% accuracy, a balanced accuracy of 96.15% and a macro-averaged F1 score of 96.54%, with a test loss of 0.1119. The gap between overall accuracy and balanced accuracy is only 0.90 percentage points, which indicates that the model does not trade minority-class performance for majority-class accuracy. The confusion matrix is dominated by the diagonal, and the errors that do occur are concentrated in the classes a buyer is most likely to encounter in the wild. The largest single confusion is Audi being read as Rolls Royce, three cases out of 199, which is understandable given that the two cars share a front-grille shape that dominates a photograph taken at an angle. Hyundai Creta is the weakest class, with a recall of 89.55% and an F1 score of 92.31%, and it is also the class with the fewest test images; its errors are spread over Rolls Royce, Tata Safari and Toyota Innova, the other high-bodied vehicles in the collection. Tata Safari shows the mirror image behaviour, with the highest recall of all classes at 99.06% and the lowest precision at 94.59%, so it absorbs some of the compact-SUV confusions. All seven classes fall between 89.55% and 99.06% recall, so the class re-weighting introduced during training is doing what it was introduced to do. The confidence gate of 0.60 was applied to the predictions in the interface: on well-separated categories the softmax output is close to one and the gate never rejects a prediction, while it becomes active on genuinely ambiguous photographs, typically those taken from an oblique angle or in poor light. This is the intended behaviour for a decision-support tool: a refusal is more useful to a buyer than a confident misidentification.

Both regressions were fitted with the same protocol. The listings are split into a training part of 80% and a test part of 20% using a grouped split on the pair of model name and price, so that a listing and its repost cannot fall on opposite sides of the boundary. The fitted coefficients are compared against a mean-predictor baseline fitted on the same training part, and the stability of the estimate is assessed with a five-fold grouped cross-validation performed inside the training part only. The results are summarised in Table 3. The year model has a clearly positive slope: a listing is worth about 77.41 million VND more for each additional year of production, which is consistent with the direction a buyer would expect. These numbers answer RQ3, and the answer is a negative one with a clear interpretation. Neither attribute explains more than five percent of the price variance, so neither can support a valuation of an individual car. The models retain value in a different role: they quantify the market’s price gradient, and they establish the scale of the noise against which any future, richer model would have to demonstrate improvement. A multivariable model that adds brand, body style, transmission and origin is the natural next step, and the body-style comparison suggests that the largest share of the missing explanatory power lies there.

The prototype demonstrates that the three capabilities can be combined without interfering with one another, and that each is useful within a well-defined range. Rule-based parsing isolates the attribute constraints reliably and reduces the corpus to candidate sets of a few dozen or a few thousand entries. The two retrieval representations are genuinely complementary, as the trim query shows: the semantic score finds the vehicle that fits the description, and the lexical score finds the vehicle that carries the requested designation. The classifier is the strongest component by a wide margin, and it stays balanced across the seven classes despite a threefold imbalance in the training data. Two engineering properties make the results reproducible rather than merely plausible: the cache key is derived from the dataset fingerprint and the model name, so a cached embedding can never be silently reused for a different corpus or model; and the retrieval engine degrades rather than fails, so the application remains usable offline.

The limitations are of four kinds, because they call for different remedies. The first is a modelling limitation in the retrieval stage: because query and listing are encoded independently, the embedding space compresses the distinction between adjacent trim codes, and the trim query in Table 1 demonstrates the consequence. This is a limitation of the bi-encoder design itself and cannot be repaired by tuning the fusion weight; the remedies are either a cross-encoder reranking stage that scores query and candidate jointly, or a rule that extracts the alphanumeric trim token from the listing title and matches it exactly. The second is a limitation of the data: the corpus contains 3,533 reposted listings, its attribute fields are missing at rates from 0.01% for the transmission to 22.95% for the distance travelled, and the price field has a long tail in which the most expensive listing is priced at 63,568 million VND, fifty times the median, so a handful of such records dominate any sum of squared errors. The third is a limitation of the evaluation: three benchmark queries cannot support a statistical claim about ranking quality, and a proper evaluation would require a labelled set of queries with relevance judgements. The classification evaluation is on a published test split never used for training, which makes it trustworthy, but the collection covers seven categories that are all popular vehicles in India and none of which is common in Vietnam, so the reported accuracy should not be read as an estimate of performance on Vietnamese traffic. The fourth is a limitation of scope: the price models are descriptive baselines rather than valuation models, and nothing in the interface uses a regression output to modify a ranking score, because the
values in Table 3 do not justify such an adjustment.

This report has built and evaluated a prototype that supports car search, car recognition and price orientation for the Vietnamese second-hand market. The three pipelines are decoupled and share a single cleaned listing table of 15,442 records. On the retrieval side, the hybrid engine recovers the intended listing exactly whenever the request is categorical, and the three benchmark queries show that the semantic and lexical components fail in different and complementary ways; the trim case documents the residual weakness of an independently encoded query and identifies the concrete remedy. On the recognition side, transfer learning proved to be the decisive choice: a compact MobileNetV2 head on a frozen-then-fine-tuned ImageNet backbone reaches 97.05% accuracy and 96.54% macro-F1 on 813 unseen photographs, with a balanced accuracy within one percentage point of the overall accuracy despite a threefold class imbalance. On the price side, the negative result is equally informative: single-variable ordinary least squares explains 4.7% of the price variance in production year and 0.8% in odometer reading, so a single attribute cannot value a car, and the price track should be used as an orientation aid and a data-quality diagnostic rather than as a scoring mechanism. Taken together, the results suggest that the value of such a system lies less in the sophistication of any single model than in making several weak signals legible to a user at once, together with the reasons why each suggestion was made.

All three components are implemented in Python and run without a GPU. The experiments were run on a laptop with an Apple M5 processor and 16 GB of memory, using Python 3.14.7, TensorFlow 2.22, scikit-learn 1.9.1, sentence-transformers 6.2.0, pandas 3.0.6, NumPy 2.5.3, Matplotlib 3.11.2 [6] and Streamlit 1.66.0 [15]. The listing data and the seven-class image collection are public, and the trained classification model together with its metrics is published under a pinned commit so that the reported numbers can be reproduced exactly rather than re-trained approximately. Three directions for future work follow from the analysis above.

Replace the bi-encoder with a two-stage pipeline that adds a cross-encoder reranking stage over the top candidates, or extract the alphanumeric trim token from the listing title and promote it to a hard filter. Either change addresses the trim confusion documented in Table 1 directly.

Extend the price analysis to a multivariable model that conditions on brand, body style, transmission, fuel type and origin, using the grouped split throughout and reporting the improvement over the single-variable baselines of Table 3.

Build a labelled query set with relevance judgements so that retrieval quality can be measured rather than illustrated, and calibrate the confidence threshold of 0.60 on a validation set drawn from Vietnamese vehicles rather than from the Indian categories of the current collection.
